episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: What gets lost when something gets easier?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down [Williams Lake Tribune] Williams Lake First Nation Competition Pow Wow brings healing love and laughter and [Williams Lake Tribune] Budget 2027: Williams Lake City Council direct staff uphold services, 0% tax rate, plus 1 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: When storytelling tools become easier to use, what institutional knowledge and editorial judgment disappears along with the difficulty, and how do newsrooms maintain that skill? Topics include: Whether AI tools should replace editorial review processes or be adopted with human filters built in from the start, How experienced editors catch subtle errors and judgment calls that tools cannot, and whether this skill can be transmitted to the next generation, The gap between what complex stories actually say (Cowichan title decision) versus how they get simplified and spread faster in compressed form, The role of institutional knowledge, local context, and community understanding (pow wow protocol) that doesn't exist in AI training data, The economic pressure on regional newsrooms to cut entry-level positions rather than invest in deliberate apprenticeship training.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Cariboo Chilcotin Partners for Literacy

articles.title: [Columbia Journalism Review] The 69-Year-Old Rookie
articles.summary: I was a fifty-year newspaper veteran and a journalism professor. Then I joined the Salt Lake Tribune as a junior editor.

discussion.central_question: When storytelling tools become easier to use, what institutional knowledge and editorial judgment disappears along with the difficulty, and how do newsrooms maintain that skill?
discussion.riley_position: AI tools are expanding faster than newsrooms can safely adopt them, but the real crisis isn't whether the tools work today—it's whether the judgment and pattern recognition that experienced editors develop over decades gets deliberately taught to the next generation, or allowed to die with institutional memory.
riley_key_evidence: A sixty-nine-year-old copy editor with fifty years of experience caught a subtle judgment error that no tool would have caught, demonstrating that pattern recognition and contextual judgment develop over time and can't be automated

The Cowichan Aboriginal title decision coverage showed how faster, cheaper storytelling (without the friction of actual explanation) spreads wrong versions faster than corrections—compression and speed beat nuance

Microsoft's Copilot logs showed the leading commercial AI tool barely reproduces full sentences from Times journalism, suggesting the underlying skill of original reporting isn't disappearing as fast as feared
discussion.casey_position: Standing outside AI adoption hasn't protected anyone from the legal and financial fights already underway, but running toward it without safeguards has produced substantial errors; the real unresolved problem is how to train the next generation of editors when entry-level tasks that used to teach judgment get handed to machines instead of junior hires.
casey_key_evidence: The BBC tested its own AI tools and found a 'confused cocktail of errors'—wrong facts stitched into plausible copy, misrepresented sourcing, and invented details that sound real
A fall study found AI assistants misrepresenting news content in a substantial share of test cases, with wrong sourcing, invented details, and stale information presented as current
Regional papers like the Tribune have thin staffing with no bench of juniors coming up behind experienced editors learning the trade by doing the boring parts of it
discussion.resolution: Riley and Casey identified two separate gaps rather than resolving them: one about whether AI is replacing reporting skill (less dire than feared), and one about institutional knowledge loss when nobody documents or trains the judgment that lives in one person's head and their contact list. They ended by asking listeners directly whether any Cariboo outlet is asking these questions or just adopting cheaper tools and hoping the problem solves itself.
topics_covered: Whether AI tools should replace editorial review processes or be adopted with human filters built in from the start
How experienced editors catch subtle errors and judgment calls that tools cannot, and whether this skill can be transmitted to the next generation
The gap between what complex stories actually say (Cowichan title decision) versus how they get simplified and spread faster in compressed form
The role of institutional knowledge, local context, and community understanding (pow wow protocol) that doesn't exist in AI training data
The economic pressure on regional newsrooms to cut entry-level positions rather than invest in deliberate apprenticeship training
calls_to_action: If you work at a paper, station, or any outlet where words get reviewed before publication, email feedback at cariboo signals dot c-a and tell us how you're training the next person to catch what you catch—this is a direct question to listeners about current practices.
Go read something with an editor behind it—Casey's closing suggestion to seek out work that has undergone human editorial review.

Newsrooms should consider building an actual junior position doing editorial tasks a machine could handle, kept on purpose so judgment gets built in a human being over years, rather than just adopting cheaper AI subscriptions.

Cariboo Chilcotin Partners for Literacy's model of person-to-person teaching should be applied to newsroom judgment training: deliberate apprenticeship built on purpose instead of hoped for by accident.

Document institutional knowledge—when reporters like the pow wow specialist move on, their understanding of protocol, tone, community context, and contact lists should be recorded formally rather than disappearing with them.
